Q000252.stem: Every insert, update, or delete in a DynamoDB orders table must trigger processing within seconds, in order per order ID, with before and after images available to the consumer. Which design fits?

choices.text: A Lambda function scanning the table every minute for changes
A CloudWatch alarm on the table's consumed write capacity
An S3 export of the table every hour processed by Glue
DynamoDB Streams (NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES) with a Lambda mapping

Q000252.explanation:
Why this is correct:
DynamoDB Streams captures item-level changes in order per partition key, and the NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES view type provides both images. A Lambda event source mapping processes records within seconds.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scanning: expensive and misses intermediate changes.
• Hourly export: not near real time.
• Capacity alarm: signals volume, not individual changes.

Key takeaway: item-level change events → Streams + Lambda.

Q000253.stem: After a full load of an on-premises Oracle database to S3, ongoing changes must keep flowing to S3 with minutes of latency until cutover, with no custom code. Which approach fits?

choices.text: A Glue job that reruns a full extract every hour
Nightly Oracle Data Pump exports copied to S3
A Snowball Edge device shipped weekly with new data
A DMS full load plus CDC task to an S3 target

Q000253.explanation:
Why this is correct:
DMS can perform a full load and then capture ongoing changes (CDC) from Oracle logs, writing them continuously to S3 targets.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Nightly exports: day-level latency.
• Hourly full extracts: heavy load and still delayed.
• Snowball: offline, not continuous.

Key takeaway: ongoing replication → DMS CDC.

Q000254.stem: Marketing needs Salesforce opportunities copied to S3 hourly, only changed records, with field mapping and filtering, and without writing code or running servers. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS DataSync with a Salesforce location
Amazon AppFlow with incremental transfer
An EC2 cron script using the Salesforce SDK
A Glue job calling the Salesforce REST API

Q000254.explanation:
Why this is correct:
AppFlow is a managed integration service for SaaS applications such as Salesforce, supporting scheduled incremental transfers, field mapping, and filters to destinations such as S3.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Glue with the REST API: custom code.
• EC2 cron: servers and code.
• DataSync: file and object storage, not SaaS APIs.

Key takeaway: SaaS → AWS without code → AppFlow.

Q000255.stem: A Glue job must start within seconds when a file lands under s3://raw/orders/, but only for .csv files, and must not start twice for the same object. Which design fits?

choices.text: A CloudWatch alarm on the bucket's object count
A Glue trigger that runs the job every five minutes
S3 events to EventBridge, filtered to start the job
A crawler scheduled every minute that starts the job

Q000255.explanation:
Why this is correct:
S3 can send events to EventBridge, where rules filter on prefix and suffix and start a Glue job or workflow. Idempotency (for example, job bookmarks or tracking processed keys) prevents double processing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Five-minute schedule: not within seconds.
• Crawler every minute: catalogs schemas, not a trigger mechanism.
• Object count alarm: coarse and delayed.

Key takeaway: event-driven ETL starts → S3 events via EventBridge.

Q000257.stem: A team already has 40 Airflow DAGs using Python operators and wants to move them to AWS without rewriting, with managed scaling and patching. Which service fits?

choices.text: Airflow self-managed on EC2 instances
AWS Step Functions with each DAG rewritten as ASL
Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow
AWS Glue workflows replacing the Airflow DAGs

Q000257.explanation:
Why this is correct:
MWAA runs Apache Airflow as a managed service, so existing DAGs and operators can move with minimal change while AWS handles infrastructure.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Step Functions rewrite: requires rewriting every DAG.
• Glue workflows: limited to Glue jobs and crawlers.
• Self-managed: patching and scaling remain your job.

Key takeaway: existing Airflow → MWAA.

Q000261.stem: Hundreds of IoT gateways write readings to one Kinesis stream, and multiple consumers (analytics, alerting, archive) read the same data independently at full speed. Which patterns describe this?

choices.text: Batch uploads to S3 processed by a nightly job
Point-to-point queues from each gateway to each consumer
Fan-in to the stream; fan-out to consumers
Fan-out from gateways; fan-in to consumers via polling

Q000261.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Many producers writing to one stream is fan-in. Several independent consumers each reading the full stream is fan-out, and enhanced fan-out gives each consumer dedicated throughput.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Reversed terms: incorrect.
• Point-to-point: an explosion of connections.
• Nightly batch: not streaming.

Key takeaway: many-to-one = fan-in; one-to-many = fan-out.

Q000263.stem: A stream job computes a 5-minute rolling average per device and must survive restarts without losing the window. What kind of processing is this, and what supports it?

choices.text: Batch processing in a nightly Glue job
Stateless filtering at the Firehose stage with a Lambda transform
Stateless processing with a Lambda per record
Stateful processing with checkpointed state (Flink)

Q000263.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Windowed aggregations keep state across records. Managed Service for Apache Flink manages keyed state and checkpoints/snapshots so windows survive restarts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Stateless Lambda: no built-in window state.
• Nightly batch: not rolling in real time.
• Firehose filtering: stateless transformation.

Key takeaway: windows and aggregations → stateful streaming.
services: Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink

Q000266.stem: New CSV folders arrive daily with occasional new columns. The team needs tables discoverable in Athena and a nightly job converting them to Parquet. Which Glue components do what?

choices.text: A crawler does both cataloging and Parquet conversion
An ETL job catalogs schemas; a crawler converts to Parquet
DataBrew catalogs; the crawler converts the files
Crawler catalogs schemas; an ETL job converts to Parquet

Q000266.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Crawlers infer schemas and update the Data Catalog, and ETL jobs read, transform, and write data such as converting CSV to Parquet.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Swapped roles: crawlers don't transform data.
• Crawler doing both: crawlers don't write data files.
• DataBrew cataloging: DataBrew prepares data; crawlers catalog.

Key takeaway: crawlers describe data; jobs change data.

Q000267.stem: A nightly Spark job processes 40 TB of logs using custom JARs and Spark tuning. The team wants the lowest cost and no cluster running between runs. Which option fits?

choices.text: A permanently running EMR cluster sized for peak
Amazon Redshift, loading 40 TB before each query
Lambda functions processing each log file in parallel on a schedule
A transient EMR cluster (or EMR Serverless) with Spot

Q000267.explanation:
Why this is correct:
EMR supports custom Spark configuration and JARs. Transient clusters or EMR Serverless avoid idle cost, and Spot capacity lowers compute cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Permanent cluster: pays for idle time.
• Redshift: a warehouse, not a Spark engine.
• Lambda: limits make 40 TB Spark-style processing impractical.

Key takeaway: big Spark batch without idle cost → transient EMR or EMR Serverless.

Q000271.stem: A Glue job must read from SQL Server on premises over Direct Connect, with no internet exposure. Which configuration fits?

choices.text: A crawler run from the internet-facing Glue endpoint
A Glue job without a connection, using the public DNS name
A Glue JDBC connection in your VPC subnet
A public endpoint for SQL Server allowed from Glue's IPs

Q000271.explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Glue connection specifies a VPC, subnet, and security group, so the job's ENIs run in your VPC and reach on-premises databases over Direct Connect or VPN routes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public endpoint: violates no internet exposure.
• Crawler from the internet: same problem.
• No connection: the job can't reach private networks.

Key takeaway: private data sources → Glue connection in your VPC.

Q000272.stem: An analyst's desktop BI tool must query Redshift Serverless securely with the analyst's corporate identity, without a shared database password. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Redshift ODBC/JDBC driver with IdP federation
Share the admin user's password with each analyst
Export the tables to CSV and email them to analysts
Query through the Data API with the root user

Q000272.explanation:
Why this is correct:
BI tools connect to Redshift through its ODBC or JDBC drivers, which support IAM or identity provider federation, so each analyst uses their own identity with temporary credentials.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Shared admin password: no accountability.
• CSV exports: stale and insecure.
• Root user: never for routine access.

Key takeaway: desktop BI → driver + federated identity.

Q000275.stem: A few-KB JSON file lands a few times per hour and must be normalized within seconds, with near-zero cost when idle. Which option fits?

choices.text: A Lambda function triggered by the S3 event
An EC2 instance polling the bucket every few seconds
An EMR cluster running continuously
A Glue Spark job started for each file

Q000275.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Lambda starts in milliseconds, scales to zero, and handles small transformations cheaply when triggered by S3 events.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Glue Spark per file: startup overhead and minimum billing for tiny files.
• EMR continuous: idle cost.
• EC2 polling: idle cost and delay.

Key takeaway: tiny, sporadic transforms → Lambda.

Q000276.stem: Athena queries on a CSV data lake scan full files though they select 5 of 80 columns, and most filter by date. Which change cuts cost MOST?

choices.text: Convert to partitioned, compressed Parquet
Convert the files to JSON Lines
Increase the Athena workgroup's data scan limit
Gzip the CSV files in place

Q000276.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Parquet is columnar and compressed, so Athena reads only the needed columns. Partitioning by date prunes files. Together these can reduce scanned data dramatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Gzip CSV: smaller files but still full-row scans.
• JSON: row-based and larger.
• Scan limit: caps usage, doesn't reduce it.

Key takeaway: Athena cost = bytes scanned → columnar + partitions.

Q000277.stem: Internal apps need a secured REST endpoint returning curated customer aggregates stored in S3, with per-app throttling and IAM auth. Which design fits?

choices.text: An EC2 web server with a shared password
Direct Athena access granted to each internal application
API Gateway with a Lambda backend querying the data
Public S3 URLs for each aggregate file

Q000277.explanation:
Why this is correct:
API Gateway provides the REST interface with IAM authorization and throttling, and Lambda queries or reads the curated data (for example, via Athena or pre-built files).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public S3 URLs: no auth or throttling.
• Direct Athena: not a REST API, and grants broader access.
• EC2 with a shared password: operational overhead and weak security.

Key takeaway: data as a secured API → API Gateway + Lambda.

Q000284.stem: Analysts run a handful of ad hoc queries each month against 5 TB of historical Parquet in S3. They want no infrastructure and cost only when querying. Which option fits?

choices.text: Athena, paying per data scanned
Loading the data into RDS for PostgreSQL
A permanent EMR cluster with Presto
A provisioned Redshift cluster running all month

Q000284.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Athena is serverless and charges by data scanned, which fits infrequent queries on data already in S3.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Provisioned Redshift: pays around the clock.
• Permanent EMR: idle cost.
• RDS load: unsuitable for 5 TB analytics.

Key takeaway: occasional queries on S3 → Athena.

Q000287.stem: A pipeline combines RDS order rows, JSON clickstream events, and product images. Which data characteristic drives the need for different storage and processing tools?

choices.text: Velocity of the order database's writes
Veracity of the clickstream's source systems
Variety of data structures
Volume of the RDS database alone

Q000287.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Variety describes different data structures (tables, JSON, images), each needing suitable formats, stores, and processing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Velocity: speed of arrival.
• Veracity: trustworthiness.
• Volume: size.

Key takeaway: different shapes of data = variety.

Q000288.stem: A pipeline calls five AWS APIs in sequence, retries failed steps with backoff, branches on results, and waits for a Glue job to finish, all without servers. Which service fits?

choices.text: A cron job on EC2 calling the AWS CLI
A single Lambda function that sleeps between API calls
AWS Step Functions with service integrations
MWAA running on the largest environment size

Q000288.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Step Functions orchestrates AWS APIs with built-in retries, branching, and .sync integrations that wait for jobs such as Glue to complete.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Sleeping Lambda: 15-minute limit and paid waiting.
• MWAA: possible but heavier for a handful of steps.
• EC2 cron: servers and custom retry logic.

Key takeaway: serverless orchestration of AWS calls → Step Functions.

Q000293.stem: When a pipeline fails, on-call engineers need an email and a remediation Lambda must run, both from one published message, each independently. Which service fits?

choices.text: An SNS topic with email and Lambda subscriptions
An SQS queue read by both the engineers and Lambda
A Kinesis stream consumed by an email client
A CloudWatch dashboard linked from the runbook

Q000293.explanation:
Why this is correct:
SNS fans out one message to multiple subscribers, such as email and Lambda, each receiving a copy.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SQS: each message is consumed once, not by both.
• Kinesis: not an email notification tool.
• Dashboard: passive.

Key takeaway: one event, many recipients → SNS.

Q000294.stem: A producer generates tasks faster than a Lambda transformer can handle, and tasks are lost when Lambda throttles. Tasks must never be lost and should be processed as capacity allows. Which change fits?

choices.text: Increase the Lambda timeout to 15 minutes
Call Lambda synchronously in a tight retry loop
Add more memory to the Lambda function
SQS between producer and Lambda, with a DLQ

Q000294.explanation:
Why this is correct:
SQS buffers tasks durably, Lambda polls at a controlled concurrency, and a DLQ captures messages that repeatedly fail.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Longer timeout: doesn't solve throttling.
• Tight retries: add pressure.
• More memory: doesn't add concurrency capacity.

Key takeaway: decouple producers from consumers with a queue.

Q000298.stem: A workflow must validate 3,000 files independently in parallel, with a concurrency limit and a failure tolerance of 1%. Which Step Functions feature fits?

choices.text: A Wait state between each file
A Choice state looping over the file list
A Parallel state with 3,000 hard-coded branches
Distributed Map with concurrency and failure limits

Q000298.explanation:
Why this is correct:
The Map state iterates over items in parallel. Distributed mode scales to large item counts from S3, with concurrency limits and a tolerated failure threshold.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Parallel with 3,000 branches: fixed branches, not dynamic iteration.
• Choice loop: sequential and slow.
• Wait: only delays.

Key takeaway: iterate items in parallel → Map (Distributed for scale).

Q000300.stem: A failed Step Functions execution must be diagnosed: which state failed, its input and output, and the error. Where is this fastest?

choices.text: AWS Config timeline for the state machine
CloudTrail event history for StartExecution
Cost Explorer for the workflow's charges
The execution's event history and graph view

Q000300.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Step Functions records each state transition with inputs, outputs, and errors, and the console highlights the failed state on the graph.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudTrail: API calls, not state details.
• Config: configuration changes.
• Cost Explorer: billing.

Key takeaway: workflow debugging → execution history.

Q000305.stem: A transformation needs custom Python UDFs, iterative feature logic, and joins over 2 TB, which is hard to express in SQL. Which option fits BEST?

choices.text: Athena SQL with nested subqueries
PySpark on Glue or EMR
A single Lambda function in Python
Redshift stored procedures only

Q000305.explanation:
Why this is correct:
PySpark scales Python logic across a cluster, supports UDFs and complex iterative transforms, and handles terabyte-scale joins.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Athena SQL: awkward for iterative Python logic.
• Single Lambda: memory and time limits.
• Stored procedures: SQL-bound and require loading into Redshift.

Key takeaway: complex Python logic at scale → PySpark.

Q000306.stem: Engineers overwrite each other's Glue scripts shared by email, with no review or history. Which practice fixes this?

choices.text: A weekly meeting to merge changes manually
Git with branches, pull requests, and CI deployment
Editing scripts only in the Glue console with job versioning
One shared S3 folder with versioning for scripts

Q000306.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Git provides history, branching, and code review, and CI/CD deploys reviewed scripts to Glue consistently.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 versioning: keeps copies but has no review or merge.
• Console edits: no review.
• Weekly meetings: slow and error-prone.

Key takeaway: treat pipeline code like application code.

Q000308.stem: A Glue job fails intermittently. The team must find error patterns across thousands of log lines from many runs and count them by error type. Which tool fits?

choices.text: CloudWatch Logs Insights queries
S3 server access logs
The Glue console's job run list
CloudTrail event history

Q000308.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Glue writes driver and executor logs to CloudWatch Logs, and Logs Insights can filter and aggregate across runs and streams.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Job run list: status, not log analysis.
• CloudTrail: API calls.
• S3 access logs: bucket requests.

Key takeaway: search and aggregate logs → Logs Insights.

Q000309.stem: A team wants pipeline infrastructure (buckets, Glue jobs, IAM roles) defined in Python with reusable components and unit tests, deployed via CloudFormation. Which tool fits?

choices.text: AWS Config rules
Systems Manager Parameter Store
AWS Service Catalog
AWS CDK

Q000309.explanation:
Why this is correct:
The CDK lets you write infrastructure in Python with constructs and tests, then synthesizes CloudFormation.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config: compliance.
• Service Catalog: distributes products.
• Parameter Store: configuration values.

Key takeaway: IaC in a programming language → CDK.

Q000310.stem: An ingestion API (API Gateway, Lambda, DynamoDB) must be defined concisely, tested locally, and deployed with gradual Lambda traffic shifting. Which framework fits?

choices.text: Elastic Beanstalk
AWS SAM
AWS OpsWorks
AWS Config

Q000310.explanation:
Why this is correct:
SAM offers shorthand serverless resources, local testing (sam local), and built-in gradual deployments with CodeDeploy (DeploymentPreference).

Why the other options are wrong:
• OpsWorks: configuration management.
• Config: compliance.
• Beanstalk: web apps on instances.

Key takeaway: serverless apps → SAM.

Q000316.stem: A script on a Windows EC2 instance must move files between local folders and S3 each night using AWS cmdlets. Which scripting language fits natively?

choices.text: SQL scripts run by the instance
Bash scripts run directly by the Windows command shell
JSON documents executed by the OS
PowerShell with AWS Tools for PowerShell

Q000316.explanation:
Why this is correct:
PowerShell is native to Windows, and AWS Tools for PowerShell provide S3 cmdlets.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Bash: not native on Windows.
• SQL: queries databases.
• JSON: data, not scripts.

Key takeaway: Windows automation → PowerShell.

Q000317.stem: Analysts need complex SQL joins and aggregations over billions of rows with concurrency for 200 users and consistent performance. Which store fits?

choices.text: Amazon DynamoDB
Amazon RDS for MySQL
Amazon ElastiCache
Amazon Redshift

Q000317.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Redshift is a columnar MPP data warehouse designed for large analytical queries, with features such as concurrency scaling.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DynamoDB: key-value access, not complex SQL.
• ElastiCache: in-memory cache.
• RDS MySQL: OLTP, not billions-row analytics.

Key takeaway: analytics at scale → data warehouse.

Q000322.stem: Partners must upload files by SFTP into S3 with their existing keys, and each partner may see only its own folder. No servers should be managed. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS DataSync agents at each partner
Transfer Family SFTP with scoped home folders
S3 presigned URLs emailed daily
An EC2 SFTP server syncing to S3

Q000322.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Transfer Family provides managed SFTP endpoints backed by S3, with users mapped to scoped IAM roles and logical home directories.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EC2 SFTP: servers to run.
• Presigned URLs: not SFTP.
• DataSync agents: not a partner SFTP service.

Key takeaway: managed SFTP into S3 → Transfer Family.

Q000324.stem: A dashboard runs the same heavy aggregation on a Redshift fact table every minute, and the base table changes a few times per hour. Which feature fits BEST?

choices.text: A UNLOAD of the table to S3 each minute
Result caching disabled to force fresh results
A materialized view with auto refresh
A bigger cluster to run the query faster

Q000324.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Materialized views store precomputed results and can refresh incrementally (auto refresh), so dashboards read small precomputed data instead of re-aggregating.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disabling the cache: more work.
• Bigger cluster: costs more for repeated work.
• UNLOAD each minute: wasteful and not a query speedup.

Key takeaway: repeated heavy aggregation → materialized views.

Q000329.stem: A team needs Spark and Hive with specific open-source versions and custom bootstrap actions, on a cluster it can tune. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Glue with its default settings
Amazon Athena SQL
AWS Batch with a generic container
Amazon EMR

Q000329.explanation:
Why this is correct:
EMR offers control over open-source application versions, configuration, and bootstrap actions for Spark, Hive, and more.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Glue: managed Spark with less control over versions and cluster tuning.
• Athena: SQL only.
• Batch: generic jobs; you'd install and manage Spark yourself.

Key takeaway: control over big-data frameworks → EMR.

Q000331.stem: Athena, EMR, Redshift Spectrum, and Glue jobs all need the same table definitions for S3 data. What provides this?

choices.text: S3 object tags describing each column
The Glue Data Catalog as a shared metastore
A README file in each bucket prefix
Each engine keeping its own local metastore

Q000331.explanation:
Why this is correct:
The Glue Data Catalog stores databases, tables, schemas, and locations, and is used by Athena, EMR (as a Hive metastore), Redshift Spectrum, and Glue.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Local metastores: definitions diverge.
• Object tags: not schemas.
• README files: not machine-readable metadata.

Key takeaway: one catalog for many engines → Glue Data Catalog.

Q000333.stem: Raw JSON with an evolving schema lands daily. Tables must appear in Athena automatically, and new fields should be added without breaking queries. Which feature fits?

choices.text: A Lambda function that edits the table DDL by hand
Athena CTAS each morning to rebuild the table
A scheduled Glue crawler with a schema update policy
A Glue ETL job that deletes and recreates tables

Q000333.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Crawlers infer schemas, including nested JSON, and their schema change policy controls how new columns are added to existing tables.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Recreating tables: breaks consumers.
• Daily CTAS: rewrites data unnecessarily.
• Manual DDL edits: fragile.

Key takeaway: schema discovery → crawlers.

Q000335.stem: Business users must find curated datasets using business terms, see ownership and quality, and request access that owners approve. Which service fits?

choices.text: The Glue Data Catalog console alone
AWS Config resource inventory with tags
Amazon SageMaker Catalog (DataZone-based)
An S3 bucket listing in the console

Q000335.explanation:
Why this is correct:
SageMaker Catalog (built on DataZone) provides business glossary, metadata, search, and publish-subscribe access workflows for governed data sharing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Glue catalog alone: technical metadata without business workflows.
• Config: resource inventory.
• Bucket listing: no metadata or requests.

Key takeaway: business data discovery and access requests → SageMaker Catalog.

Q000339.stem: A daily job must export a Redshift query result to S3 as Parquet, partitioned by date, in parallel. Which command fits?

choices.text: INSERT INTO an external table only
A SELECT run from the query editor with results downloaded
UNLOAD with FORMAT PARQUET and PARTITION BY
COPY with FORMAT PARQUET

Q000339.explanation:
Why this is correct:
UNLOAD writes query results to S3 in parallel, supports Parquet, and can partition output by columns.

Why the other options are wrong:
• COPY: loads data into Redshift.
• External table insert: possible in some cases but not the standard export tool described.
• Query editor: not an export mechanism.

Key takeaway: export from Redshift → UNLOAD; load → COPY.

Q000340.stem: Several gzip CSV files in S3 must be loaded into a Redshift table quickly using all slices. Which approach fits?

choices.text: COPY from many split files
One huge single file loaded by COPY
UNLOAD from S3 into the table
Individual INSERT statements for each row

Q000340.explanation:
Why this is correct:
COPY loads in parallel across slices. Splitting data into multiple files (ideally a multiple of the slice count) maximizes parallelism.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Row INSERTs: very slow.
• One huge file: limits parallelism.
• UNLOAD: exports, not loads.

Key takeaway: bulk load → COPY from many files.

Q000342.stem: A DynamoDB table stores sessions that must disappear 24 hours after creation, without consuming write capacity for deletes, and deletions must be archived to S3. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Switching the table to on-demand capacity
A scheduled Lambda that scans and deletes items
A GSI keyed on the creation timestamp for expired items
TTL, with Streams capturing expirations for archive

Q000342.explanation:
Why this is correct:
TTL deletes expired items without consuming write capacity. Those deletions appear in DynamoDB Streams, where Lambda can archive them to S3.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scan and delete: consumes capacity and costs more.
• On-demand: billing mode only.
• GSI: doesn't delete anything.

Key takeaway: automatic expiry → TTL; archive via Streams.

Q000354.stem: An Oracle data warehouse moving to Redshift has PL/SQL procedures and Oracle-specific types that must be converted, with a report on items needing manual work. Which tool fits?

choices.text: AWS Glue crawlers over the Oracle schemas
Redshift COPY commands
AWS DMS full load alone
AWS SCT (or DMS Schema Conversion)

Q000354.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Schema conversion tools convert schemas and code between engines and produce an assessment report of objects needing manual effort. DMS then moves the data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DMS alone: moves data, not code conversion.
• Crawlers: catalog schemas.
• COPY: loads data.

Key takeaway: heterogeneous schema/code conversion → SCT or DMS Schema Conversion.

Q000356.stem: Auditors ask which dataset version, processing job, and training job produced a deployed model, and which endpoints use it. Which capability fits?

choices.text: CloudTrail event history
SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking
S3 Inventory reports on the model artifact bucket
AWS Config timeline

Q000356.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Lineage Tracking records entities (datasets, jobs, models, endpoints) and their relationships, so you can trace a model back to its inputs and forward to deployments.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudTrail: API calls without artifact relationships.
• S3 Inventory: object lists.
• Config: resource configuration.

Key takeaway: artifact relationships → Lineage Tracking.

Q000361.stem: A RAG app's knowledge base returns irrelevant chunks for questions phrased differently from the documents' wording. What role does the embedding model play, and what fixes this?

choices.text: It generates the final answer; a larger LLM fixes this
It compresses documents for storage; more compression fixes this
It translates queries; turning translation off fixes this
It maps text to vectors for semantic search; choose a suitable one

Q000361.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Embeddings represent meaning as vectors so similar meanings are close even with different wording. Choosing a domain-appropriate embedding model (and good chunking) improves retrieval.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Answer generation: that's the LLM, not the embedding model.
• Compression: not the role.
• Translation: not the role.

Key takeaway: retrieval quality depends on embeddings and chunking.

Q000363.stem: A workflow runs Glue jobs, an EMR step, and Lambda, with conditional branches, retries, and waits for completion, and must be visualized for operators. Which fits?

choices.text: A single Glue trigger
A cron job on an EC2 instance
An EventBridge rule per step
AWS Step Functions

Q000363.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Step Functions integrates with Glue, EMR, and Lambda (including run-to-completion patterns), supports branching and retries, and shows each execution visually.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EventBridge rules per step: event wiring without workflow state.
• Glue trigger: limited to Glue.
• EC2 cron: custom logic and servers.

Key takeaway: cross-service workflows with state → Step Functions.

Q000365.stem: A Python Lambda function must start a Glue job with runtime arguments whenever a message arrives, and record the run ID. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Invoke the Glue job through its S3 script URL
Use CloudFormation to create a new job each time
Call glue.start_job_run() with Boto3
Put the arguments in an SNS topic for Glue

Q000365.explanation:
Why this is correct:
The Boto3 Glue client's start_job_run accepts the job name and arguments and returns a JobRunId.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 script URL: not an invocation method.
• SNS to Glue: Glue doesn't subscribe to SNS.
• Creating jobs per run: unnecessary.

Key takeaway: call AWS services from code via the SDK.

Q000367.stem: Before building a pipeline, an engineer wants to profile a new dataset visually (nulls, distributions, outliers) and try cleaning steps without code. Which tool fits?

choices.text: Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose
Amazon Athena
AWS Glue DataBrew
AWS Glue crawler

Q000367.explanation:
Why this is correct:
DataBrew provides visual data profiling and 250+ transformations, saved as recipes that can run as jobs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Crawler: schema only.
• Athena: SQL, no visual profiling.
• Firehose: streaming delivery.

Key takeaway: visual profiling and cleaning → DataBrew.

Q000368.stem: Data engineers, analysts, and ML engineers want one workspace for SQL, notebooks, data prep, and model building on governed data, with shared projects. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio
Amazon QuickSight
AWS Cloud9 with shared environments
AWS Glue Studio

Q000368.explanation:
Why this is correct:
SageMaker Unified Studio brings together data processing, SQL analytics, and ML/AI development in project-based collaborative workspaces with governed data access.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Glue Studio: ETL authoring only.
• QuickSight: BI dashboards.
• Cloud9: a general IDE.

Key takeaway: one workspace for data + analytics + AI → Unified Studio.

Q000370.stem: A validation function must run the moment objects are created under incoming/, and a second team also wants the same events without changing the first setup. Which design fits?

choices.text: S3 events to EventBridge, one rule per consumer
The Lambda function polling the bucket
A crawler running every minute over incoming/
CloudTrail Insights on the bucket's write activity

Q000370.explanation:
Why this is correct:
EventBridge receives S3 object-created events and lets multiple rules route them to independent targets, such as each team's Lambda.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Crawler: catalogs; doesn't trigger validation.
• Polling: delay and cost.
• CloudTrail Insights: anomaly detection.

Key takeaway: multiple consumers of S3 events → EventBridge.

Q000372.stem: Executives need interactive drill-down dashboards, while an engineer must profile and clean raw data visually first. Which pair fits?

choices.text: Athena for both dashboards and profiling
QuickSight for dashboards; DataBrew for profiling
DataBrew for dashboards; QuickSight for profiling
CloudWatch dashboards for executives; Glue crawlers for cleaning

Q000372.explanation:
Why this is correct:
QuickSight builds interactive BI dashboards. DataBrew profiles and cleans data visually.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Swapped: each tool in the other's role.
• Athena: queries only.
• CloudWatch/crawlers: operational metrics and schema discovery.

Key takeaway: BI → QuickSight; visual data prep → DataBrew.

Q000374.stem: An engineer wants to run Python cells interactively on a sample, inspect DataFrames, plot results, and document findings for teammates. Which fits?

choices.text: A CloudFormation template
A Lambda function with print statements
A Glue ETL job run on a schedule
A Jupyter notebook in SageMaker Studio

Q000374.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Notebooks support interactive execution, inline outputs and charts, and documentation cells, which suits exploration and sharing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scheduled ETL: not interactive.
• Lambda prints: not exploratory.
• CloudFormation: infrastructure.

Key takeaway: interactive exploration → notebooks.

Q000377.stem: Analysts use Athena SQL but need Python transformations with Spark libraries on the same S3 data, without managing clusters. Which capability fits?

choices.text: Athena SQL user-defined functions only
Athena for Apache Spark notebooks
Redshift Spectrum
A permanent EMR cluster

Q000377.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Athena for Apache Spark runs PySpark interactively in notebooks within Athena, serverlessly, against data in S3.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SQL UDFs: limited compared to Spark.
• EMR: cluster management.
• Spectrum: SQL from Redshift.

Key takeaway: serverless interactive Spark → Athena for Spark.

Q000380.stem: Each file must be checked immediately after upload for header row and row count before the pipeline proceeds, and failures must stop the next stage. Which design fits?

choices.text: A nightly crawler that checks headers
An Athena query run weekly
A full EMR job per file for validation
An S3-triggered validation Lambda

Q000380.explanation:
Why this is correct:
A lightweight Lambda triggered by the upload performs quick checks and reports success or failure (for example, by moving the file or emitting an event) so downstream stages proceed only on valid files.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Nightly crawler: late, and crawlers don't validate.
• EMR per file: heavy.
• Weekly query: too late.

Key takeaway: light, immediate checks → event-triggered Lambda.

Q000381.stem: Security must find who deleted a Glue table and from which IP two weeks ago. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS CloudTrail
AWS Glue job bookmarks
Amazon CloudWatch metrics
Amazon Macie

Q000381.explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudTrail records API calls such as glue:DeleteTable, with identity, time, and source IP; event history keeps 90 days of management events.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Metrics: no caller identity.
• Bookmarks: track processed data.
• Macie: sensitive data.

Key takeaway: who did what → CloudTrail.

Q000382.stem: A Glue Spark job failed. Where are the driver and executor logs, and how can failures be seen by stage?

choices.text: On the Glue console home page only
CloudWatch Logs; the Spark UI shows stages
In CloudTrail data events for the job's S3 reads
In the job's S3 script location

Q000382.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Glue sends driver and executor logs to CloudWatch Logs (continuous logging can stream them during the run). The Spark UI, enabled with event logs, shows stages and tasks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Script location: holds code.
• CloudTrail: API calls.
• Console home: summaries only.

Key takeaway: Glue logs → CloudWatch; Spark detail → Spark UI.

Q000383.stem: The team must be emailed within minutes whenever any Glue job fails or times out. Which setup fits?

choices.text: A daily Athena query over job history
EventBridge job-state rule → SNS email
A CloudTrail trail with S3 delivery
AWS Config rule on Glue jobs

Q000383.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Glue emits job state change events to EventBridge. A rule matching FAILED or TIMEOUT states can publish to an SNS topic with email subscriptions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Daily query: too slow.
• CloudTrail: API calls, not job states.
• Config: configuration compliance.

Key takeaway: job state alerts → EventBridge + SNS.

Q000388.stem: Application logs stream in, and engineers need full-text search and interactive visualizations within seconds of ingestion. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon OpenSearch Service with Dashboards
Amazon Athena over logs delivered to S3
Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL
Amazon Redshift

Q000388.explanation:
Why this is correct:
OpenSearch indexes logs for near-real-time full-text search and provides dashboards for visualization.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Redshift: analytics, not full-text log search.
• Athena: queries files in S3 after delivery.
• RDS: not designed for log search at scale.

Key takeaway: interactive log search → OpenSearch.

Q000390.stem: Operations wants a monthly trend of successful versus failed Glue job runs, with an alarm if failures exceed 5 in an hour. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Job-state events as metrics, with an alarm
AWS Config compliance history
S3 server access logs on the script bucket
VPC Flow Logs from the Glue ENIs

Q000390.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Glue job state change events in EventBridge can feed counts into CloudWatch metrics (for example, via a rule and Lambda, or Glue's job observability metrics), which support trends and alarms.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 logs: script access.
• Config: configuration.
• Flow logs: network traffic.

Key takeaway: job outcome trends → events turned into metrics.

Q000394.stem: A Spark join on customer_id runs one task for 2 hours while the others finish in minutes. One customer has 40% of the rows. What is happening, and what helps?

choices.text: Too many executors; reduce the cluster size
Data skew; salt the hot key or use AQE skew joins
Network timeouts; raise the timeout values
Insufficient partitions for small keys; merge files

Q000394.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Skew puts a disproportionate share of data in one partition. Salting the hot key or enabling Spark's adaptive query execution skew-join handling spreads the work.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Fewer executors: makes it slower.
• Timeouts: symptom, not cause.
• Merging files: doesn't fix key skew.

Key takeaway: one slow task + hot key = skew.

Q000397.stem: A Lambda function reads from s3://raw/ and writes to s3://curated/. Security requires least privilege and no long-term keys. Which setup fits?

choices.text: An IAM user's access keys in environment variables
A role with only the needed Get/Put permissions
AmazonS3FullAccess on the execution role
Public bucket policies so no IAM is needed

Q000397.explanation:
Why this is correct:
The execution role provides temporary credentials, and scoping actions and resources to exactly what's needed applies least privilege.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Access keys: long-term credentials.
• Full access: over-privileged.
• Public buckets: exposes data.

Key takeaway: scope role permissions to actions and resources.

Q000398.stem: A Redshift admin password must rotate every 30 days, and applications must keep working without code changes. Which approach fits?

choices.text: A calendar reminder to change the password manually
Secrets Manager automatic rotation; apps fetch the secret
Parameter Store standard parameters with no rotation
KMS automatic key rotation on the cluster

Q000398.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Secrets Manager rotates supported database credentials on a schedule and updates the secret, so applications that retrieve the secret at runtime keep working.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual change: error-prone.
• Parameter Store: no built-in rotation.
• KMS rotation: rotates encryption keys, not passwords.

Key takeaway: password rotation → Secrets Manager.

Q000401.stem: A team compares PostgreSQL on RDS with PostgreSQL on EC2 for a pipeline database. Which responsibility split is correct?

choices.text: Both: AWS patches everything, including your SQL
EC2: AWS patches the OS; RDS: you patch the engine
Both: you patch the hypervisor and host hardware
RDS: AWS patches OS and engine; EC2: you patch both

Q000401.explanation:
Why this is correct:
With RDS, AWS manages the OS and database engine patching (in maintenance windows). On EC2, the customer owns the OS and database software. Customers always manage their data, access, and network settings.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS patching EC2's OS: customer responsibility.
• AWS patching everything: data and access remain yours.
• Hypervisor: always AWS.

Key takeaway: managed services move patching to AWS.

Q000405.stem: An app needs a database password that rotates, plus a non-secret batch-size setting that changes occasionally, at the lowest cost. Which split fits?

choices.text: Both in Parameter Store SecureString without rotation
Both in Secrets Manager
Password in Secrets Manager; setting in Parameter Store
Both hardcoded in the application

Q000405.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Secrets Manager provides rotation for credentials. Parameter Store standard parameters are free and fit plain configuration.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Both in Secrets Manager: pays for non-secret config.
• SecureString without rotation: misses the rotation need.
• Hardcoded: inflexible and insecure.

Key takeaway: secrets with rotation vs. plain config: different stores.

Q000408.stem: A new analyst needs SELECT on two schemas in Redshift and nothing else, and future tables in those schemas should be readable too. Which approach fits?

choices.text: An IAM policy granting redshift:*
A superuser account for the analyst
A role with USAGE, SELECT, and default privileges
The admin user's credentials

Q000408.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Database privileges are granted with GRANT (USAGE on schema, SELECT on tables) to roles or groups. ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES covers tables created later.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Admin credentials and superuser: over-privileged.
• redshift:*: IAM control-plane actions, not table privileges.

Key takeaway: table-level access in Redshift = SQL GRANTs.

Q000412.stem: Data scientists query a Redshift table with names and SSNs. They must see masked SSNs, while a compliance role sees full values, from the same table. Which feature fits?

choices.text: KMS encryption of the SSN column with a separate key
Redshift dynamic data masking policies by role
A separate masked copy of the table per team
Row-level security on the table only

Q000412.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Dynamic data masking applies masking policies at query time based on the user's role, so the same table returns masked or full values.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Masked copy: duplication and sync issues.
• KMS encryption: at-rest protection; authorized queries see plaintext.
• Row-level security: filters rows, not column values.

Key takeaway: role-based column masking → dynamic data masking.

Q000414.stem: A requirement states that data must be encrypted before leaving the application and that AWS services must only ever store ciphertext. Which approach fits?

choices.text: SSE-KMS on the destination bucket
TLS for data in transit only
SSE-S3 default encryption
Client-side encryption

Q000414.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Client-side encryption encrypts data in the application before sending it, so services store only ciphertext.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SSE-KMS and SSE-S3: the service encrypts after receiving plaintext.
• TLS: protects transit only.

Key takeaway: encrypt before sending → client-side encryption.

Q000423.stem: Logs from many sources must be centralized for interactive search, dashboards, and anomaly alerts within seconds. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Glue streaming ETL
Amazon OpenSearch Service
Amazon Redshift
Amazon Athena

Q000423.explanation:
Why this is correct:
OpenSearch provides indexing, search, dashboards, and alerting and anomaly detection plugins for near-real-time log analytics.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Redshift: batch-oriented analytics.
• Athena: queries files after delivery.
• Glue: ETL.

Key takeaway: log analytics platform → OpenSearch.

Q000424.stem: A producer Redshift workgroup must give a consumer team in another account live read access to three schemas, without copying data or building ETL. Which feature fits?

choices.text: A DMS task replicating the tables
UNLOAD to S3 and COPY into the consumer
Redshift data sharing (cross-account)
A nightly snapshot restored in the consumer account

Q000424.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Data sharing grants live, read-only access to databases, schemas, or tables across clusters or workgroups, including across accounts, without moving data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• UNLOAD/COPY: copies data and adds latency.
• Snapshot restore: a copy and stale.
• DMS: replication and cost.

Key takeaway: share live data without copies → data sharing.

Q000426.stem: After a pipeline broke, the team needs to see when a bucket policy and a Glue connection were changed, and what the previous settings were. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Config configuration history
Amazon CloudWatch metrics
Amazon Macie bucket inventory
AWS Trusted Advisor

Q000426.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Config records resource configurations over time and shows what changed and when, alongside related CloudTrail events.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Metrics: performance, not configuration.
• Macie: sensitive data.
• Trusted Advisor: best-practice checks.

Key takeaway: what was the configuration before? → Config.
